subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Herd Behavior
description: A short lesson to help you apply Herd Behavior.

hook.text: In 1999, everyone bought internet stocks because everyone else was buying. By 2001, the market had lost $5 trillion.

buildup.text: Herd behavior: we follow the crowd because we assume others know something we do not. It feels safe to follow.

discovery.text: Information cascades form: early movers act, followers copy, and the chain grows even when nobody has good information.

twist.text: The herd can be right sometimes. But when it is wrong, everyone crashes together. Diversified thinking beats crowds.

climax.text: Before following the crowd, ask: do I've independent evidence or am I just copying? The distinction matters enormously.

punchline.text: A crowd is not a reason. It is just a crowd.

quiz.question: What drives an information cascade?
options: Everyone independently analyzing the same data
Early movers act and followers copy without independent evidence

details.summary: Herd behavior occurs when individuals follow the actions of a larger group rather than making independent decisions. In financial markets, herding creates bubbles and crashes as investors buy because others are buying and sell because others are selling.
details.whyItMatters: Herding amplifies market volatility, creates speculative bubbles, and causes panicked selloffs that have little relationship to underlying fundamentals.
takeaways: People copy the crowd especially when uncertainty is high
Herding creates bubbles when buying attracts more buying
Independent analysis is the antidote to herd-driven decisions

faq.question: Why do intelligent people follow the herd?
faq.answer: In uncertain situations, observing what others do provides real information. If many people are buying, they might know something you do not. The problem is that they may also be following others who are following others, creating an information-free cascade.

faq.question: How does herding create financial bubbles?
faq.answer: Rising prices attract buyers. Their buying pushes prices higher, attracting more buyers. Each participant sees the rising price as validation. The true cause is circular: prices rise because people buy, and people buy because prices rise. This loop continues until reality intervenes.
